questions.explain: The four leak paths are query leakage (mitigated by RLS), retrieval leakage (tenant predicates with vector ordering), prompt leakage (session binding), and inference leakage (keep sensitive data out of shared-model prompts).
options: Query, retrieval, prompt, and inference leakage — each with its own mitigation
Only SQL injection
Only insider threats
Only network eavesdropping
questions.q: What is the chapter's threat model for memory leaks?

questions.explain: User-grain predicates (SESSION_CONTEXT user_id) guard personal memory tables; tenant-grain predicates guard the shared corpus; support staff use a separate login with an is_support predicate — never policy exceptions.
options: One policy for all tables with no grain distinction
Tenant-grain for everything
User-grain for personal memory tables, tenant-grain for the shared corpus, separate support predicate for staff
RLS is not needed if the app filters correctly
questions.q: How are the two RLS grains applied across memory tables?

questions.explain: usp_bind_session validates session ownership from the JWT subject claim, stamps both tenant_id and user_id into SESSION_CONTEXT, and no database work happens before it succeeds — it is the choke point of every turn.
options: It runs once at user registration
It validates session ownership from the JWT subject, stamps both identities into SESSION_CONTEXT, and gates all database work
It only checks the session status
It replaces RLS entirely
questions.q: What does usp_bind_session do and why is it the choke point?

questions.explain: Application code still passes explicit identity predicates (sargable, intent obvious); the API login gets only EXECUTE on procedures with DENY on direct memory-table writes; least-privilege roles per role limit blast radius.
options: RLS alone is sufficient; skip app predicates
Give the API login db_owner for simplicity
Disable RLS during business hours
Explicit app predicates plus RLS backstop, with least-privilege roles (EXECUTE-only API login, DENY direct writes)
questions.q: What is the application-layer defense beyond RLS?

questions.explain: The CI suite covers cross-user read attempts, missing-context simulation (NULL context must return zero rows), vector-search tenant separation, and session-fixation attempts — because isolation regressions are silent.
options: Manual testing once a year
Only load testing
Adversarial CI tests: cross-user reads, missing context, vector-search isolation, session fixation
Trusting RLS without tests
questions.q: What does the adversarial isolation test suite cover?
